newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK RPI to fall back, start downward trend.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK RPI to fall back, start downward trend.

text.p: Headline inflation in Britain is expected to have subsided in December having shown disturbing signs of heading up in recent months.
Annual retail price inflation is forecast by a Reuter poll of economists to have sidled down to 2.6 percent in December despite rising by 0.5 percent on the month.
That could signal the start of a new downward path for price pressures, albeit gradual.
RPI leapt to 2.7 percent year-on-year in October, from 2.1 the month before, and then held there in November.
The figures will be released at 0930 GMT on Thursday.

The Reuter poll of economists forecast underlying inflation, excluding mortgage interest payments, will also have dropped to 3.1 percent year-on-year, having spent the previous two months at 3.3 percent.

"The peak in underlying inflation could be behind us although the prospects for the government achieving its target...by the end of this parliament look remote," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc.
The government has a medium-term target of 2.5 percent for annual underlying inflation.
Shaw said the effects of measures introduced by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke in his November budget would show through in December's inflation figures.

Increased duties on petrol, tobacco and vehicle excise duties would add about 0.2 or 0.3 percent to the overall inflation figures, he said. That tallied with the overall consensus forecast for a 0.5 percent rise in RPI on the month.
Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said budget measures, falling food prices and the pound's strength would all play their part in December.

"A variety of factors are at work this month, including a drop in food price inflation and a lower excise duty impact than last year, particularly as some areas such as petrol will be affected by sterling's appreciation," he said.

Barr said petrol prices would rise only 3.5 percent in the year to December, compared with more than seven percent growth in 1995. The pound has leapt more than 14 percent on a trade-weighted basis since taking off last August.

Producer prices, released on Monday, showed pipeline inflation pressures remain dormant. Output prices rose 0.5 percent in December and 1.7 percent year-on-year. That was the lowest annual rate of increase since October 1996.
But the threat to headline inflation lies not in background pressures but with the temptation for high street retailers to try and rebuild price margins after years of being squeezed.
"Sharp increases in both clothing and household goods prices last month provide evidence that retailers are nudging up margins in the face of firmer consumer demand," Shaw said.
Clothing and footwear prices jumped 1.1 percent in November while household goods were only just behind, rising 1.0 percent.
But evidence of subdued sales over the Christmas period suggests consumers remain price-sensitive.

The British Retail Consortium's December sales monitor, released overnight, showed like-for-like sales grew 4.3 percent in value, down from November's 4.9 percent rate of growth and the 5.9 percent increase seen in October.
Anecdotal evidence suggests the January sales period has started with a bang, however.

Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International, said the January sales period would probably prove to be strong, counterbalancing a subdued pre-Christmas period, as consumers waited for prices to be cut before spending. "You've got to look at December and January together to judge the retail sales trend," he said.
